subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation and low-flow first-line
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 5 month old boy referred by his general practitioner on day 3 of coryza and cough. He is exclusively breastfed and has taken about half his usual feeds over the last 12 hours. He is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. He has no personal or family history of asthma, no prior wheeze, and was born at 39 weeks by unremarkable vaginal delivery.

On examination he has moderate subcostal recession and audible wheeze with widespread fine inspiratory crackles. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for respiratory syncytial virus. Vital signs: pulse 158/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 58/min, SpO2 88% in room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and mucous membranes are moist. Bedside blood glucose is 4.6 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal recession; widespread wheeze and fine inspiratory crackles; alert and consolable
data_table.Feeding: Approximately 50% of usual breastfeeds in the last 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Begin high-flow nasal cannula humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg/min as first-line escalation
options.rationale: HFNC is not first-line in RCH bronchiolitis: only after a 2 hour low-flow trial has failed to maintain adequate oxygenation or work of breathing does HFNC start; starting HFNC before this exposes the infant to unnecessary intensive-level care (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Give one dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg while observing on room air
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in acute viral bronchiolitis under 12 months; delaying oxygen while trialling steroid leaves a hypoxic infant untreated (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with oxygen driving gas as an initial airway measure
options.rationale: RCH explicitly recommends against nebulised bronchodilators in bronchiolitis under 12 months because they do not alter length of stay or oxygen requirement, and they distract from the correct oxygen escalation pathway (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent or above
options.rationale: The RCH bronchiolitis pathway makes low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min the first-line intervention, with SpO2 target of 90 percent or above; escalation to HFNC is reserved for children who fail low-flow after a 2 hour trial (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Administer nebulised hypertonic 3 percent saline before adjusting inspired oxygen
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH pathway for typical bronchiolitis and has no evidence of reducing admission or ICU escalation; oxygen delivery to correct hypoxaemia takes precedence (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: The RCH bronchiolitis pathway sets a graded oxygen ladder: low-flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min first, with SpO2 target of 90 percent, then HFNC only after failure of a 2 hour low-flow trial. Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, and corticosteroids are not routinely used because they do not change hard outcomes and can distract from the oxygen escalation that actually matters. In this alert, well perfused 5 month old with an SpO2 of 88 percent, low-flow nasal prong is both proportionate and protocol-adherent.
key_points: Bronchiolitis first-line oxygen is low-flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, target SpO2 at least 90 percent
HFNC only after a documented failed 2 hour low-flow trial
Nebulised bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, and corticosteroids are not recommended
explanation.pearls: RCH accepts SpO2 as low as 90 percent in bronchiolitis without escalating; over-oxygenation prolongs admissions without changing outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid rate with cerebral oedema risk balance
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9 year old boy with new-onset type 1 diabetes. He presented with 2 weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and a 4 kg weight loss. He has been vomiting for 12 hours and is drowsy but rousable. His mother reports no headache and no visual complaints before arrival.

Weight today is 28 kg. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 26 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.4), sodium 132 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), and beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 100 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds and mucous membranes are dry. GCS is 14.

data_table.Weight and vitals: 28 kg; HR 130; BP 96/58; RR 34 Kussmaul; SpO2 100 percent; T 36.9
data_table.VBG: pH 7.14; HCO3 8 mmol/L (22 to 32); glucose 26 mmol/L; Na 132 mmol/L; K 4.8 mmol/L; beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Neurology: GCS 14; drowsy but rousable; no headache or visual complaints

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid regimen?

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 15 minutes, then deficit plus maintenance over 24 hours
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus and 24 hour rehydration is deprecated in paediatric DKA because faster fluid delivery is associated with cerebral oedema; RCH and ISPAD both cap the initial bolus at 10 mL/kg in the absence of shock (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/h before starting any intravenous fluid replacement
options.rationale: Insulin is deferred by 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins because starting insulin before restoring intravascular volume drives potassium intracellularly and worsens hypovolaemia and cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes, then deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours
options.rationale: APEG and RCH paediatric DKA guidance sets an initial isotonic bolus of 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes for haemodynamically stable moderate to severe DKA, followed by rehydration of the assumed 7 to 10 percent deficit plus maintenance evenly across 48 hours to reduce cerebral oedema risk (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: Give oral rehydration solution with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin for 4 hours before intravenous access
options.rationale: Oral rehydration and subcutaneous insulin are not appropriate for moderate to severe DKA with drowsiness and vomiting; delaying intravenous rehydration risks progression to shock and cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

options.text: 5 mL/kg 0.45 percent sodium chloride bolus over 60 minutes with an 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate infusion
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid is avoided in the resuscitation phase and bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia because it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CNS acidosis (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management deliberately uses smaller boluses (10 mL/kg over 30 minutes) and longer rehydration (48 hours) than adult protocols because cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/h starts an hour after fluid begins, never before. Bicarbonate is reserved for cardiac-arrest-level acidosis. Hypotonic fluids are avoided during resuscitation because they worsen the drop in serum osmolality that drives cerebral oedema.
key_points: 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus over 30 minutes for non-shocked moderate to severe DKA
Deficit plus maintenance replaced evenly over 48 hours
Insulin infusion starts 1 hour after fluid; bicarbonate almost never indicated
explanation.pearls: In children with DKA, keep the fluid slow: rapid rehydration and hypotonic fluids are the two biggest reversible cerebral oedema risks.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and HHS

subtopic_detail: Febrile infant under 3 months workup thresholds
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a metropolitan tertiary emergency department. A previously well 6 week old girl born at term is brought in by her father because she felt hot to touch and has been feeding less over the last 8 hours. He measured a rectal temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius at home. She has had no cough, no rash, and no exposure to unwell contacts, and her immunisations are up to date for age.

On examination she is alert with a strong cry, pink and well perfused, and hydrated. There is no focal source. Vital signs: pulse 168/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius. Anterior fontanelle is soft and flat.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168; BP 78/44; RR 46; SpO2 99 percent; T 38.5
data_table.Examination: Alert with strong cry; well perfused and hydrated; no focal source; soft flat fontanelle
data_table.History: 6 weeks old, term birth, immunisations up to date; reduced feeds 8 hours; rectal T 38.4 at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation and empirical treatment plan?

options.text: Observe in the short-stay unit for 4 hours and reassess before deciding on any investigations
options.rationale: Watchful waiting under 3 months delays diagnosis of bacteraemia and meningitis; the guideline mandates immediate investigation and empirical antibiotics rather than observation before a workup (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).

options.text: Full septic workup including lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: RCH sepsis guidance treats any infant under 3 months with fever as high risk regardless of appearance; the standard is full workup including LP with empirical IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover early neonatal pathogens and community bacteria (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).

options.text: Reassure the family the child is well and arrange a general practitioner follow-up in 24 hours
options.rationale: Well appearance in an infant under 3 months does not exclude serious bacterial infection; discharge without workup or antibiotics has an unacceptable miss rate for meningitis and bacteraemia at this age (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).

options.text: Urine microscopy and chest radiograph, deferring lumbar puncture unless CRP is elevated
options.rationale: CRP thresholds are used in older infants under the step-by-step approach but do not defer LP under 3 months in AU practice; RCH requires LP as part of the initial workup at this age (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).

options.text: Blood cultures and urine microscopy only, with discharge on oral amoxicillin and a next-day review
options.rationale: Omitting LP and using oral antibiotics is not acceptable under 3 months because meningitis cannot be excluded clinically at this age and oral absorption is unreliable; RCH mandates parenteral therapy and full workup (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child).

explanation.summary: Infants under 3 months with any documented fever above 38.0 degrees Celsius are managed as possible sepsis regardless of clinical appearance because clinical assessment misses invasive bacterial infection at this age. The RCH pathway mandates a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover community pathogens and residual neonatal organisms such as Listeria and group B streptococcus. Observation, oral antibiotics, and CRP-first deferral of LP are inconsistent with this pathway.
key_points: Fever under 3 months triggers full septic workup even when the infant looks well
LP is part of the initial workup, not deferred pending CRP
Empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers Listeria and community pathogens
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 3 months, the well appearance is not reassurance; the age itself is the risk factor and the workup runs regardless.

subtopic_detail: Simple febrile seizure workup and disposition
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl in the emergency department 90 minutes after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes at home. She has been coryzal for 2 days and reached a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius shortly before the seizure. She returned to her baseline within 20 minutes and has since been playing with a toy at triage. Her immunisations are up to date and there is no family history of epilepsy.

On examination she is alert and interactive with clear rhinorrhoea, red pharynx without exudate, and no rash. Neurological examination including tone, gait, and cranial nerves is normal. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130; BP 98/62; RR 28; SpO2 99 percent; T 38.4
data_table.Seizure: Generalised tonic-clonic, 3 minutes, single, resolved 90 minutes ago
data_table.Examination: Alert, interactive; normal neurology; coryzal features; no rash
data_table.Background: Immunisations up to date; no family history of epilepsy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone before considering discharge
options.rationale: LP is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure in a well child aged 18 months without meningism; the RCH criteria specifically identify this presentation as low risk and mandate no lumbar puncture (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Order an urgent outpatient EEG within 1 week to exclude an underlying epilepsy syndrome
options.rationale: EEG has no role after a first simple febrile seizure; it does not change management and has a false-positive rate that generates unnecessary anxiety (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Commence daily oral sodium valproate 20 mg/kg/day as long-term seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended after simple febrile seizures; the modest reduction in recurrence does not justify long-term drug exposure in a benign self-limiting condition (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Prescribe rectal diazepam for the family to give at the onset of any future febrile illness
options.rationale: Prophylactic benzodiazepines at fever onset are not routine after a first simple febrile seizure and expose the child to sedation without changing meaningful outcomes; rescue midazolam is reserved for prolonged or recurrent complex seizures (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

options.text: Give antipyretic advice, reassure the family, and discharge with GP review
options.rationale: This meets RCH criteria for a simple febrile seizure (generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, age 6 months to 5 years, back to baseline); no bloods, no imaging, no LP, no EEG is indicated and safe discharge with parental education is the standard (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizure).

explanation.summary: A simple febrile seizure in a child aged 6 months to 5 years is generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, and followed by return to baseline. RCH policy is no bloods, no imaging, no LP, and no EEG for children meeting these criteria who look well. Discharge with antipyretic advice and a written safety net is the standard. Rescue medication is reserved for children with prolonged or recurrent complex febrile seizures. Long-term prophylaxis is not warranted.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: generalised, under 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, baseline return
No LP, EEG, imaging, or prophylactic antiepileptic required
Discharge with education about recurrence and antipyretic use
explanation.pearls: Recurrence of febrile seizures is common (about 1 in 3) but does not increase epilepsy risk enough to warrant prophylaxis.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease supplemental criteria and IVIG threshold
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 2 year old boy in a regional hospital on day 6 of fever above 39 degrees Celsius. He is fractious and difficult to console. His parents describe a red patchy rash on the torso that came and went on day 3, and cracked lips that his father has been putting balm on. He has been drinking half his usual volume.

On examination there is bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue, and cracked lips. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Peripheral extremities show mild erythema of the palms without desquamation. Vital signs: pulse 148/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius. Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105 to 135), white cells 18 x 10^9/L (5 to 15), platelets 480 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), CRP 92 mg/L (under 5), ESR 68 mm/h (under 20), albumin 28 g/L (33 to 47), ALT 74 U/L (under 40), and urinalysis shows 40 leucocytes per high-power field with a sterile culture.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148; BP 92/58; RR 30; SpO2 99 percent; T 39.4
data_table.Clinical criteria present: Fever day 6; bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis; strawberry tongue with cracked lips; palmar erythema
data_table.Missing classical criteria: No cervical lymphadenopathy >=1.5 cm; rash resolved by day 3; no desquamation yet
data_table.Laboratory: Hb 96; WCC 18; platelets 480; CRP 92; ESR 68; albumin 28; ALT 74
data_table.Urinalysis: Sterile pyuria 40 leucocytes per high-power field

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day for 3 days as first-line therapy alone
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line; steroids are added to IVIG only in high-risk children (Kobayashi score suggestive of IVIG resistance) and never replace IVIG in initial treatment (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Order blood culture, urine culture, and chest radiograph and wait 24 hours before any specific therapy
options.rationale: The child meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria today; withholding IVIG for 24 hours of culture surveillance costs a treatment window that reduces coronary aneurysm risk and does not add diagnostic information the current data does not already give (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Treat empirically for occult bacterial infection with intravenous ceftriaxone and defer immunoglobulin
options.rationale: The clinical picture with sterile pyuria and mucocutaneous features fits Kawasaki not bacterial sepsis; antibiotics without IVIG leave the coronary risk untreated and can be given alongside IVIG when infection is a genuine competing possibility (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Arrange echocardiography and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day now
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever for at least 5 days is accompanied by 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory findings (CRP 30 mg/L or above, ESR 40 mm/h or above, and 3 or more of anaemia, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, elevated ALT, sterile pyuria, leucocytosis); this child meets both and IVIG should not wait for confirmation to minimise coronary aneurysm risk (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Continue observation with paracetamol and reassess on day 10 with repeat inflammatory markers
options.rationale: Delaying IVIG past day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; a child meeting incomplete Kawasaki criteria on day 6 needs treatment now, not further observation (Source: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease).
source_refs: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease requires fever for at least 5 days plus 2 to 3 clinical criteria and supportive laboratory findings. The AHA algorithm activates when CRP is at least 30 mg/L or ESR at least 40 mm/h plus three of anaemia, thrombocytosis above 450, albumin below 30, ALT above the reference range, leucocytes above 15, or sterile pyuria. This 2 year old satisfies both the clinical and laboratory arms. Coronary aneurysm risk is minimised when IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is given before day 10, so delay for further culture or observation is unsafe.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever plus 2 to 3 criteria plus supportive labs triggers immediate treatment
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day reduces coronary aneurysm risk when given before day 10
Steroids are adjunct in high-risk children (Kobayashi score), never a replacement for IVIG
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria, thrombocytosis, and hypoalbuminaemia are the three most useful Kawasaki labs that support an incomplete presentation; a normal ESR does not exclude Kawasaki when CRP is high.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease
